Receptor Pharmacology - PANCE Summary 
Adrenergic, Cholinergic, Histamine, Serotonin, Dopamine, GABA, Opioid, NMDA, AT1, Mineralocorticoid, Leukotriene 
PANCE relevance:   Pharmacology is tested under   Pharmaceutical Therapeutics (15%)   and   Applying Foundational Scientific Concepts (8%)   - mechanism of action, indications, and ADRs. Drugs listed are PANCE-relevant
agents commonly prescribed clinically. 
Adrenergic (Sympathetic) Receptors 
Receptor   Location & Effect When Activated   Agonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Antagonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Key Pearls / ADRs 
α 1 
Gq (IP3/DAG)
Vascular smooth muscle, prostate /
bladder neck, iris dilator (radial muscle) 
→   Vasoconstriction, mydriasis,   ↑ 
bladder neck tone (urinary retention)
Phenylephrine   →   pressor, nasal decongestant 
Midodrine   →   orthostatic hypotension 
Oxymetazoline   →   intranasal decongestant 
Norepinephrine   →   septic shock
Non-selective:   prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin   →   HTN,
BPH, PTSD nightmares (prazosin) 
α 1A-selective:   tamsulosin, silodosin, alfuzosin   →   BPH 
Mixed   α 1/ β : carvedilol, labetalol   (see   β 2 row) 
First-dose orthostatic hypotension /
syncope 
Reflex tachycardia
Tamsulosin:   intraoperative floppy iris
syndrome   at cataract surgery 
α 2 
Gi
Presynaptic CNS sympathetic neurons;
pancreatic   β -cells 
→   ↓   sympathetic outflow,   ↓   insulin
release
Clonidine   →   HTN (resistant), ADHD, opioid
withdrawal, hot flashes 
Tizanidine   →   muscle spasticity 
Dexmedetomidine   →   ICU sedation 
Brimonidine   →   glaucoma (topical) 
Methyldopa   →   HTN in pregnancy 
Yohimbine   (rarely clinical)   Clonidine:   rebound HTN if abruptly
stopped ; sedation; dry mouth
Methyldopa: + Coombs hemolytic anemia 
β 1 
Gs (cAMP)
Heart (SA / AV / myocardium); kidney JG
cells 
→   ↑   HR,   ↑   contractility,   ↑   AV
conduction,   ↑   renin release
Dobutamine   →   cardiogenic shock,
decompensated HF 
Isoproterenol   →   bradycardia / AV block (rare)
Cardioselective ( β 1 >   β 2):   metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol,
esmolol, nebivolol 
→   HTN, HFrEF, post-MI, AFib rate control, SVT, thyroid
storm, migraine prophylaxis 
Cardioselective preferred in
asthma/COPD & diabetics 
Mask hypoglycemia symptoms
(tachycardia) - sweating preserved
Avoid abrupt withdrawal (rebound)
Contraindications: severe bradycardia,
2nd/3rd degree AV block, decompensated
HF 
β 2 
Gs
Bronchi, uterus, vascular & skeletal
muscle, liver 
→   Bronchodilation, uterine relaxation,
vasodilation,   ↑   glycogenolysis,   ↑ 
insulin 
SABA:   albuterol, levalbuterol   →   asthma rescue,
acute COPD
LABA:   salmeterol, formoterol   →   asthma
maintenance ( only with ICS ), COPD 
Terbutaline   →   tocolysis (preterm labor) 
Non-selective   β -blockers (pure   β ):   propranolol, nadolol,
timolol, sotalol 
→   Propranolol: essential tremor, performance anxiety,
thyrotoxicosis, portal HTN, migraine prophylaxis 
→   Timolol: glaucoma (topical) 
→   Sotalol: also class III antiarrhythmic (K+ blocker) for AFib 
Mixed   α 1 + non-selective   β -antagonists:   carvedilol   (PO,
HFrEF + HTN),   labetalol   (IV/PO, HTN emergency, HTN in
pregnancy/preeclampsia) 
→   α 1 blockade adds vasodilation : lowers SVR rapidly
(helpful in HTN emergency & pregnancy) and reduces
afterload (HF benefit) 
β 2 agonist ADRs:   tremor, tachycardia,
hypokalemia   (K+ shifts intracellularly),
hyperglycemia 
LABA monotherapy   →   ↑   asthma death
(black box) 
Avoid non-selective   β -blockers in asthma
Carvedilol/labetalol: orthostatic
hypotension from   α 1 component (start low,
titrate up) 
β 3 
Gs
Bladder detrusor, brown adipose 
→   Detrusor relaxation ( ↑   bladder
capacity), lipolysis
Mirabegron   →   overactive bladder (alternative to
antimuscarinics; less dry mouth)
-   Mirabegron ADR:   HTN , nasopharyngitis,
UTI
Avoid in uncontrolled HTN 
Mixed Sympathomimetics & Dopaminergics 
Drug   Receptors   Clinical Use   Pearls 
Epinephrine   α 1,   α 2,   β 1,   β 2 (all)   Anaphylaxis (1st line, IM); cardiac arrest; severe asthma; local anesthetic
vasoconstriction
Anaphylaxis dose: 0.3 mg IM (adult), 0.15 mg IM (peds <30 kg)

Drug   Receptors   Clinical Use   Pearls 
Norepinephrine   α 1,   α 2,   β 1 (minimal   β 2)   Septic shock - 1st line vasopressor   More vasoconstriction than epi; less   β 2 activity 
Dopamine   Dose-dependent: low D1   →   mid   β 1   → 
high   α 1
Shock (less common now), bradycardia   No longer 1st line for septic shock (NE preferred) 
Pseudoephedrine /
Ephedrine 
Indirect:   ↑   NE release ( α   &   β )   Nasal decongestant (pseudo); pressor (ephedrine)   Avoid in HTN; pseudoephedrine restricted (meth precursor) 
Cocaine / Amphetamines   Indirect: block reuptake /   ↑   release of
NE/DA
Toxidrome: HTN, tachycardia, mydriasis, hyperthermia   Avoid   β -blockers   in cocaine toxicity (unopposed   α   →   vasospasm); use
benzos

Cholinergic (Parasympathetic) Receptors 
Mnemonic for muscarinic effects (parasympathetic):   SLUDGE   - Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramping, Emesis. Or   DUMBBELS   - Diaphoresis, Urination, Miosis, Bronchoconstriction, Bradycardia,
Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation. 
Receptor   Location & Effect When Activated   Agonists / Cholinomimetics   Antagonists (Anticholinergics)   Key Pearls / ADRs 
Muscarinic 
(M1, M2, M3)
M1/M3: Gq
M2: Gi 
M1:   CNS (cognition), gastric parietal
cells (acid) 
M2:   Heart   →   ↓   HR,   ↓   AV conduction
M3:   Smooth muscle & glands   → 
bronchoconstriction, GI/GU motility &
secretions, miosis (sphincter),
accommodation (ciliary) 
Direct:   Bethanechol   →   postop urinary retention,
neurogenic bladder 
Pilocarpine   →   closed-angle glaucoma; xerostomia
(Sjögren, post-radiation) 
Cevimeline   →   Sjögren xerostomia
Indirect (AChE inhibitors): see next section 
Atropine   →   symptomatic bradycardia,
organophosphate poisoning, premed for secretions 
Ipratropium / Tiotropium   →   COPD, asthma 
Oxybutynin, Tolterodine, Solifenacin, Darifenacin,
Trospium   →   OAB 
Scopolamine   →   motion sickness (patch) 
Glycopyrrolate   →   perioperative secretions;
hyperhidrosis 
Benztropine, Trihexyphenidyl   →   Parkinson tremor,
EPS from antipsychotics 
Dicyclomine, Hyoscyamine   →   IBS cramping 
Anticholinergic toxidrome:   'Hot as a hare,
dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat,
mad as a hatter, full as a flask' 
= hyperthermia, dry skin/mouth, flushing,
mydriasis & blurred vision, delirium, urinary
retention 
Avoid in:   closed-angle glaucoma, BPH,
dementia (worsens cognition)
Reverse with   physostigmine   (crosses BBB)
Beers list: anticholinergics in elderly 
Nicotinic 
Ligand-gated
cation channel
Nm (NMJ)
Nn (ganglia,
adrenal medulla) 
Nm:   Skeletal muscle NMJ   → 
contraction
Nn:   Autonomic ganglia (both
sympathetic and parasympathetic),
adrenal medulla   →   epi/NE release 
Nicotine   (smoking, patch/gum) 
Varenicline   →   smoking cessation (partial agonist at 
α 4 β 2 nAChR) 
Succinylcholine   (depolarizing)   →   rapid sequence
intubation
Non-depolarizing NMJ blockers:   rocuronium,
vecuronium, cisatracurium, atracurium   → 
intubation, surgical paralysis
Reverse with   neostigmine + glycopyrrolate   or 
sugammadex   (roc/vec)
Ganglionic blockers: rare clinically 
Succinylcholine ADRs:   hyperkalemia
(avoid in burns / crush / denervation), 
malignant hyperthermia   (treat with
dantrolene), bradycardia in peds
Varenicline: vivid dreams, neuropsychiatric
(boxed warning removed 2016) 
Cholinesterase Inhibitors (Indirect Cholinomimetics) 
Drug   Use   Pearls / ADRs 
Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine   Alzheimer disease (mild-moderate; rivastigmine also for
Parkinson dementia)
ADRs: nausea, diarrhea, bradycardia, syncope, weight loss; modest symptomatic benefit only 
Neostigmine, Pyridostigmine   Myasthenia gravis (pyridostigmine = chronic outpatient);
reversal of non-depolarizing NMJ blockade (neostigmine +
glycopyrrolate)
Do not cross BBB. Cholinergic crisis if overdose   →   weakness mimicking MG flare 
Physostigmine   Reversal of   anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) toxicity   Crosses BBB   (treats CNS delirium); contraindicated in TCA overdose (seizures, asystole) 
Edrophonium   Historical 'Tensilon test' for myasthenia gravis dx (largely
replaced by anti-AChR antibody testing)
Very short-acting 
Organophosphates   (insecticides, nerve agents)   Toxicity   - irreversible AChE inhibition   SLUDGE/DUMBBELS   + muscle fasciculations + paralysis. Treat with   atropine   (muscarinic effects) + 
pralidoxime/2-PAM   (regenerates AChE) - give pralidoxime early before 'aging' 
Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic Organ Effects 
Organ   Sympathetic Effect (Receptor)   Parasympathetic Effect (Receptor) 
Heart - SA/AV/contractility   ↑   HR,   ↑   conduction,   ↑   contractility ( β 1)   ↓   HR,   ↓   AV conduction (M2) 
Vascular smooth muscle   Vasoconstriction ( α 1) / vasodilation in skeletal muscle ( β 2)   No direct innervation (endothelial NO) 
Bronchi   Bronchodilation ( β 2)   Bronchoconstriction,   ↑   secretions (M3) 
GI tract   ↓   motility & secretions ( α 2,   β 2)   ↑   motility & secretions (M3) 
Bladder - detrusor / sphincter   Detrusor relaxation ( β 3) / sphincter contraction ( α 1)   →   retention   Detrusor contraction (M3) / sphincter relaxation   →   voiding

Organ   Sympathetic Effect (Receptor)   Parasympathetic Effect (Receptor) 
Eye - pupil / ciliary   Mydriasis   ( α 1, radial muscle)   Miosis   (M3, sphincter); accommodation for near (M3, ciliary) 
Pancreas (insulin)   ↓   insulin ( α 2)   ↑   insulin (M3) 
Kidney (renin)   ↑   renin ( β 1)   -

Other PANCE-Relevant Receptors 
Histamine, Serotonin, Dopamine, GABA, Opioid, NMDA, AT1, Mineralocorticoid, Leukotriene 
Receptor   Location & Effect   Agonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Antagonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Key Pearls / ADRs
HISTAMINE 
H1 
Gq
Bronchi, vascular smooth muscle,
sensory nerves 
→   Bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, 
↑   vascular permeability, pruritus, pain 
Endogenous histamine (allergy, mast cells)   1st-gen (sedating, anticholinergic):   diphenhydramine,
hydroxyzine, promethazine, chlorpheniramine,
doxylamine, meclizine 
→   allergy, urticaria, motion sickness (meclizine,
scopolamine), insomnia (diphenhydramine), N/V
(promethazine, hydroxyzine) 
2nd-gen (non-sedating):   loratadine, cetirizine,
fexofenadine, desloratadine, levocetirizine 
→   allergic rhinitis, urticaria
1st-gen ADRs: anticholinergic toxidrome,
sedation, paradoxical excitation in peds
Avoid 1st-gen in elderly (Beers list)
Promethazine: extravasation tissue necrosis
(avoid IV; black box) 
H2 
Gs
Gastric parietal cells 
→   ↑   Gastric acid secretion 
-   Famotidine, Cimetidine, Nizatidine 
→   GERD, PUD, stress ulcer prophylaxis,
Zollinger-Ellison (less potent than PPIs) 
Cimetidine:   CYP450 inhibitor (warfarin,
phenytoin, theophylline interactions); 
antiandrogen effects   (gynecomastia, ED, 
↑   prolactin) 
Famotidine preferred   - no CYP /
antiandrogen issues
Tachyphylaxis with chronic use; PPIs more
effective for healing PUD 
SEROTONIN (5-HT) 
5-HT1B/1D   Cranial vasculature, trigeminal nerve 
→   Vasoconstriction,   ↓   CGRP release
Triptans   - sumatriptan, rizatriptan, eletriptan,
zolmitriptan 
→   acute migraine
-   Contraindicated in CAD, uncontrolled
HTN, prior stroke, hemiplegic migraine,
pregnancy 
Serotonin syndrome risk if combined with
SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs/tramadol 
5-HT1A 
Gi
CNS (anxiety, mood)   Buspirone   - partial agonist   →   generalized anxiety
disorder 
Aripiprazole   - partial agonist (also D2 partial agonist)
-   Buspirone: non-sedating, no dependence,
no withdrawal; takes 2-4 weeks for effect;
no PRN use 
5-HT2A 
Gq
CNS, platelets   LSD, mescaline (recreational)   Atypical antipsychotics:   risperidone, olanzapine,
quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, paliperidone,
lurasidone, clozapine 
Mirtazapine (also   α 2 antagonist; antidepressant +
appetite/sleep)
Trazodone (also SARI; insomnia & depression)
Atypicals   →   lower EPS than typicals but   ↑ 
metabolic syndrome (weight, T2DM, lipids) 
Clozapine:   agranulocytosis (REMS
monitoring), seizures, myocarditis -
reserved for refractory schizophrenia
Trazodone: priapism 
5-HT3 
Ligand-gated
cation
CNS (chemoreceptor trigger zone), GI
vagal afferents 
→   Emesis 
-   Ondansetron, Granisetron, Dolasetron,
Palonosetron 
→   chemotherapy-induced N/V, post-op N/V,
hyperemesis gravidarum
Mirtazapine (also blocks 5-HT3 - additional antiemetic
effect) 
QT prolongation   with ondansetron (esp.
IV); avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs
Headache, constipation 
5-HT4 
Gs
Enteric neurons 
→   ↑   GI motility
Metoclopramide   (also D2 antagonist)   →   gastroparesis,
refractory N/V 
Prucalopride   →   chronic constipation
-   Metoclopramide:   tardive dyskinesia (black
box) ; EPS; hyperprolactinemia
Avoid in bowel obstruction, Parkinson
disease

Receptor   Location & Effect   Agonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Antagonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Key Pearls / ADRs 
SSRI / SNRI 
(reuptake
inhibitors)
Presynaptic 5-HT (and NE for SNRI)
reuptake transporters 
SSRIs:   fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram,
paroxetine, fluvoxamine 
SNRIs:   venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine,
milnacipran 
→   depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD, neuropathic pain
(duloxetine), fibromyalgia
-   Sexual dysfunction, GI upset,   ↑   suicidality in
young (black box),   serotonin syndrome 
(esp. with MAOIs/triptans/tramadol/linezolid
- clonus, hyperthermia, autonomic
instability)
Discontinuation syndrome (esp. paroxetine,
venlafaxine) 
DOPAMINE 
D1 
Gs
Renal/mesenteric vasculature, direct
pathway striatum
Fenoldopam   →   hypertensive emergency (rare)
Low-dose dopamine
-   Generally less PANCE-relevant than D2 
D2 
Gi
Mesolimbic, nigrostriatal,
tuberoinfundibular pathways 
→   Modulates psychosis, movement,
prolactin (tonic inhibition)
Bromocriptine, cabergoline   - prolactinoma,
suppression of lactation 
Pramipexole, ropinirole   - Parkinson disease, restless
legs syndrome 
Levodopa/carbidopa   - Parkinson disease (precursor;
not a direct receptor agonist) 
Apomorphine   - PD off-episodes 
Aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine   - D2 partial
agonists (atypical antipsychotics)
Typicals:   haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine 
→   schizophrenia, acute psychosis, Tourette
Atypicals: see 5-HT2A row
Antiemetics:   metoclopramide, prochlorperazine,
promethazine
Tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine   (VMAT2 inhibitors) 
→   Huntington chorea, tardive dyskinesia 
Antipsychotic ADRs:   EPS (acute dystonia,
akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), 
neuroleptic malignant syndrome   (fever,
rigidity, autonomic instability,   ↑   CK; treat
with dantrolene/bromocriptine), 
hyperprolactinemia   (galactorrhea,
gynecomastia, amenorrhea), QT
prolongation
DA agonists for Parkinson: impulse-control
disorders (gambling), N/V, orthostasis,
hallucinations 
GABA 
GABA-A 
Ligand-gated
Cl -   channel
CNS, widespread 
→   Hyperpolarization (inhibitory)
Benzodiazepines   ( ↑   frequency   of Cl- channel opening):
alprazolam, lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam,
clonazepam, temazepam, oxazepam, chlordiazepoxide 
→   anxiety, panic, alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus,
insomnia, procedural sedation 
Z-drugs   ( α 1-selective): zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone 
→   insomnia 
Barbiturates   ( ↑   duration   of opening): phenobarbital   → 
status epilepticus, neonatal sz
Propofol, etomidate, ketamine adjunct, alcohol 
Flumazenil   →   benzodiazepine reversal (use cautiously
- precipitates seizures in chronic users / mixed
overdoses)
Benzo ADRs: sedation, falls in elderly,
dependence, withdrawal (seizures),
respiratory depression with opioids/alcohol 
Lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam 
('LOT'): no active metabolites - prefer in liver
disease & elderly
Barbiturates: narrow therapeutic index,
induce CYP 
GABA-B 
Gi
CNS, spinal cord 
→   Inhibitory (presynaptic)
Baclofen   →   spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury, cerebral
palsy); intrathecal pump for severe spasticity
GHB (recreational/Xyrem for narcolepsy)
-   Avoid abrupt baclofen withdrawal   → 
seizures, hallucinations, hyperthermia (esp.
intrathecal) 
OPIOID 
μ   (mu) 
Gi
(also   κ ,   δ )
CNS (analgesia, euphoria, respiratory
depression), GI 
→   Analgesia, sedation, respiratory
depression, miosis, constipation,
euphoria
Full agonists:   morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone,
hydromorphone, fentanyl, methadone, codeine,
meperidine, tramadol 
Partial agonist:   buprenorphine (Suboxone = bup +
naloxone)   →   OUD, chronic pain 
→   analgesia, OUD maintenance, cough suppression
(codeine), diarrhea (loperamide, diphenoxylate -
peripheral) 
Naloxone   (short-acting, IV/IM/IN)   →   opioid overdose
reversal 
Naltrexone   (long-acting PO/IM Vivitrol)   →   OUD & AUD
maintenance 
Methylnaltrexone, naloxegol   →   opioid-induced
constipation (peripheral, no analgesia loss) 
Triad of overdose:   respiratory depression
+ miosis +   ↓   LOC
Tolerance to all effects EXCEPT miosis &
constipation 
Methadone:   QT prolongation; long half-life 
Tramadol/Meperidine:   seizure risk &
serotonin syndrome (also SNRI activity) 
Codeine:   avoid in children (CYP2D6
ultra-rapid metabolizers)
Naloxone in chronic opioid users   → 
precipitates withdrawal 
NMDA / GLUTAMATE

Receptor   Location & Effect   Agonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Antagonists (drug   →   clinical use)   Key Pearls / ADRs 
NMDA 
Ligand-gated
cation
CNS (excitatory) 
→   Excitotoxicity in stroke /
neurodegeneration; involved in
memory (LTP) 
Glutamate (endogenous)   Memantine   →   moderate-severe Alzheimer disease 
Ketamine   →   dissociative anesthesia, refractory
depression (esketamine nasal spray), procedural
sedation 
Dextromethorphan   →   cough; abuse potential
PCP (recreational)
Memantine: well-tolerated; can combine
with AChE inhibitor 
Ketamine:   emergence reactions
(hallucinations - mitigate with benzo);   ↑ 
ICP/IOP; preserves airway reflexes;
bronchodilator (useful in asthma)
Alcohol withdrawal: NMDA upregulation
contributes to seizures/delirium tremens 
OTHER MAJOR RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST CLASSES 
AT1
(angiotensin) 
Gq
Vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex,
kidney 
→   Vasoconstriction,   ↑   aldosterone,
Na+/H2O retention 
Angiotensin II (endogenous)   ARBs:   losartan, valsartan, candesartan, olmesartan,
telmisartan, irbesartan, azilsartan 
→   HTN, HFrEF, CKD/diabetic nephropathy, post-MI 
ACE inhibitors   (block AngII formation, not receptor):
lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, benazepril   →   same
indications
Both classes:   hyperkalemia, AKI   (esp. with
bilateral renal artery stenosis),   teratogenic
(avoid in pregnancy) 
ACEi: dry cough (bradykinin), angioedema
(higher in Black patients)
ARBs: less cough/angioedema - alternative
to ACEi
Do NOT combine ACEi + ARB 
Mineralocortic
oid
(aldosterone) 
Renal collecting duct, heart, vascular
smooth muscle 
→   Na+/H2O retention, K+ excretion,
cardiac fibrosis 
Aldosterone (endogenous; pathologic in primary
hyperaldosteronism / Conn) 
Spironolactone, Eplerenone 
→   HFrEF, resistant HTN, primary hyperaldosteronism,
ascites/cirrhosis, hirsutism & acne (spironolactone),
PCOS
Both:   hyperkalemia 
Spironolactone: gynecomastia, menstrual
irregularity,   ↓   libido (eplerenone has fewer
endocrine effects)
Avoid combining with ACEi/ARB or K+
supplements without close monitoring 
Leukotriene 
(CysLT1)
Bronchi, eosinophils 
→   Bronchoconstriction, mucus,
inflammation 
Endogenous leukotrienes (esp. LTC4, D4, E4)   Montelukast, Zafirlukast   (LTRA)   →   asthma
maintenance, allergic rhinitis, exercise-induced
bronchospasm 
Zileuton   (5-LOX inhibitor)   →   asthma 
Montelukast: black box for
neuropsychiatric effects   (depression,
suicidality, sleep disturbance)
Zileuton: hepatotoxicity - monitor LFTs
Especially useful for   aspirin-exacerbated
respiratory disease (Samter triad)
